Beauhurst identifies ambitious businesses using eight triggers 
(outlined at the bottom of this page) that suggest a company has 
high-growth potential. More detail on Beauhurst’s tracking triggers

Equity investment 
To be included in the analysis, any investment must be:
• 
Some form of equity investment
• 
Secured by a non-listed UK company
• 
Issued between 1 January 2011 and 31 December 2020
Announced and unannounced fundraisings 
An unannounced fundraising is an investment made into a private 
company that is completed without press coverage or a statement 
from the recipient company or funds that made the investment. 
These transactions are an integral part of the UK’s high-growth 
economy, accounting for around 70% of all equity transactions.

New Media and Immersive Tech
We’re excited to be working with 
Beauhurst to produce this series of 
three industry reports examining 
the UK companies that will shape 
the future of how we consume 
retail, media and food. 
 
In the third of three reports, we 
focus on the New Media and 
Immersive Industries, including XR 
(Extended Reality) and The Future 
of Gaming. We’re looking at how 
brave new brands in these spheres 
are influencing the future of how 
we create and consume content, 
game, and immerse ourselves in the 
changing landscape of the online 
and digital spaces. 
The evolution of the internet is 
gathering speed, which follows a 
new wave of approaches to content 
creation and digital creativity. As 
we hurtle towards the Metaverse 
and Web 3.0, we’re taking a look 
at the new media brands, creative 
agencies and immersive tech 
companies that are rising to the 
challenge of making their mark on a 
new iteration of the internet. 
 
With increasing accessibility 
around XR technology and 
the future of gaming looking 
progressively more immersive—
the way we’re reacting to digital 
content at scale is changing. From 
online publishing and social media 
to marketing and advertising 
technology, industries across the 
sector adapt and put their lens on 
this new reality 
 
The high-growth New Media and 
Immersive Tech sector houses 
2,289 active companies. Almost 
three-quarters of these active 
companies are young, at seed 
or venture stage—a promising 
indication for the investment 
ecosystem. London is a hotspot for 
activity in the sector (1,175 active 
companies), with Brighton and 
Hove (51) showing itself as a city to 
watch. Manchester (43), Glasgow 
(42), Bristol (41), and Edinburgh 
(41) are also generating New Media 
and Immersive Tech innovation. 
The industry has collectively raised 
£4.3b of investment between 2011 
and 2020. The space is also home 
to some of the UK’s most innovative 
gaming and immersive tech brands, 
including software developer, 
Improbable, who achieved unicorn 
status in 2017. 
 
This report will home in on two 
sub-industries: XR and The Future 
of Gaming. XR encompasses 
VR (Virtual Reality) and AR 
(Augmented Reality). With 141 
active high-growth companies, 
this space has sparked investor 
curiosity around the potential of the 
technology. Between the beginning 
of 2020 and the end of November 
2021, the sector saw £45.6m equity 
investment. This amounts to 33% 
of the total funding received by the 
industry since 2011. 
 
The Future of Gaming is an exciting 
sub-industry with 401 active high-
growth companies, making it the 
dominant sub-space within New 
Media and Immersive Tech. Equity 
investment into this space has 
been plentiful, with high-growth 
companies attracting £1.46b across 
938 fundraising rounds since 2011. 
Gaming is also trending towards 
a more immersive experience 
for users, trailblazing a high-
tech path for this generation of 
gamers. The gaming industry has 
also been praised for its ability to 
reap success outside of London, 
with companies in Edinburgh 
and Nottingham reaching high 
valuations.

New Media and Immersive Tech
The world of New Media and 
Immersive Tech represents the 
continuing innovation of mass 
communication and the technologies 
that enable it. Companies that 
operate in this industry fall under the 
sectors of online publishing, social 
networks, films and TV, photography, 
videography and video content, virtual 
reality, video games, and marketing 
and advertising technology.
Among the 3,282 ambitious 
New Media companies that form 
the lifetime total of businesses 
underpinning this report, 2,289 
remain active in the high-growth 
ecosystem, 241 have exited via an 
IPO or acquisition, and the remaining 
752 are no longer in operation. Over 
a 10 year period, these companies 
have raised a total of £4.3b of equity 
investment across 4,629 deals.
Almost three quarters of the 
businesses currently active in 
the fast-growth space are young 
companies at seed or venture stage, 
indicating more opportunities for 
investors in the future. Startups in 
the full New Media cohort also have 
853 accelerator attendances between 
them—a sign of their innovative 
nature and promise for growth. In 
addition, these companies have 
received 690 grants with a combined 
value of £107m from a range of 
sources including Innovate UK, the 
Ministry of Defence, the European 
Commission, and Scottish EDGE.

New Media and Immersive Tech
The New Media and Immersive Tech 
industry holds enormous potential for 
innovating all types of media from films 
and TV to gaming and adtech. One of 
the biggest names in the New Media 
and Immersive Tech cohort is software 
developer Improbable which facilitates 
large-scale multiplayer virtual worlds; 
these have been used in gaming, but 
also have applications as synthetic 
environments simulating real world 
problems in areas such as defence. 
Launched in 2012, the company has 
secured £461m of equity fundraising and 
achieved unicorn status in 2017.
Another high-growth player in the 
gaming industry is Tripledot Studios. It 
rocketed from a pre-money valuation of 
£17.5m in 2018 up to £273m in 2021.
Other innovative companies are 
developing highly realistic characters and 
digital human faces to disrupt the gaming 
and virtual storytelling arenas, such as 
UCL spinout Synthesia and University of 
Ulster-born HUMAIN.

Over four equity rounds in 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2020, Mesmerise has 
secured a total of £1.56m of investment funding. With headquarters in 
Westminster, the quickly growing firm also increased its headcount from 
five in 2017 to 21 in 2020.

With the intention of innovating mobile apps for fitness, FitXR simulates 
the experience of the gym by developing software that creates a 
virtual fitness club. The app combines intense full body workouts with 
immersive virtual reality fitness content and classes, allowing users to 
meet and exercise with others from their own homes.
FitXR is backed by fundraising worth £6.91m, constituted by a £952k 
round in 2018 from funders TenOneTen Ventures and Maveron, and a 
£5.96m combined equity and loan deal in 2020 from the same investors 
alongside BoostVC, Hiro Capital and Innovation Loans.

7
New Media and Immersive Tech
Despite the number of deals 
somewhat in decline since 2015, 
the volume of equity investment 
secured by New Media and 
Immersive Tech companies has 
remained healthy in recent years. 
Notably, the total investment 
of £563m raised in 2020 is 
very much in the same range 
as £514m in 2019 and £641m 
in 2018, suggesting the sector 
proved reasonably resilient 
during a pandemic year.
Over the decade, 2017 saw a 
particular peak in equity volume 
due to a £389m deal secured by 
software developer Improbable 
and a £136m round raised 
by films and TV firm The Ink 
Factory. Other large deals for 
ambitious New Media companies 
in the 2011 to 2020 timeframe 
include Moonbug’s 2018 and 
2020 rounds, which were worth 
£115m and £92.5 respectively.
Around 40% of the 4,629 deals 
secured were the first time 
that the company had raised 
equity. Clear portions of the total 
£4.3b raised by high-growth 
New Media businesses went to 
emerging industries: £275m to 
Artificial Intelligence, £240m 
to AdTech, £200m to EdTech, 
£110m to virtual reality, and 
£109m to e-sports.

ry deep-dive: Extended reality
Extended reality (XR) is the 
combination of virtual reality (VR), 
where users enter immersive digital 
worlds, and augmented reality (AR), 
which combines virtual elements 
with real views for an enhanced 
experience. These technologies first 
appeared in the 1960s when the first 
head-mounted display was launched 
and the US military introduced the 
first flight stimulator. 
Within the high-growth space, 
investor interest has been spiked 
by the possibilities of XR. These 
companies have taken advantage of 
the evolving perception of human 
connection by advancing a novel 
environment in which users can 
communicate with people all over 
the world. The technology creates 
more authentic and engaging 
settings than those offered by 
traditional social media.
The COVID-19 pandemic increased 
interest in the XR industry, as 
lockdowns across the globe 
encouraged more open-minded 
attitudes towards the sector. Despite 
the easing of social distancing 
measures, the value of XR has been 
realised by many, as evidenced by 
investment trends. Since the start 
of 2020 and the end of November 
2021, the sector saw £45.6m of 
equity investment—33% of the total 
funding received by the industry 
since 2011.

Augmented reality (AR)
A key component of the XR industry is AR, 
where virtual elements are superimposed 
onto the real world, as opposed to the 
completely simulated experiences of VR. AR 
has a large number of applications across 
different sectors, from interior design 
experimentation before committing to costly 
renovation or seeing the fit of clothing before 
purchase, to training tools for medical staff 
or manufacturing workers.
Examples of high-growth companies 
operating in this space include DigitalBridge, 
which allows users to virtually decorate their 
homes to reduce retail returns and product 
waste. It has raised £4.72m of equity funding. 
Meanwhile, Sen uses AR and AI to stream 
satellite imagery of Earth and space. Sen has 
secured equity investment worth £4.25m.
Virtual reality (VR)
Despite much overlap between the two emerging 
sectors, more of the companies in the extended 
reality space are operating in VR than AR. VR refers 
to technology that creates a full immersive virtual 
environment. Creators of VR products hope to 
revolutionise lifestyle industries such as gaming, 
retail, and fitness, as well as work environments, 
including onboarding programs and virtual meetings.
Recipient of £4.73m of investment, Blend Media 
operates an online platform where users can 
upload 360º videos, access a large content library 
and connect with immersive technology experts. 
Games company MeetspaceVR operates a virtual 
gaming arena where players use their bodies 
as a game controller.It is backed by £2.45m of 
equity investment. Also in the VR gaming space 
is storytelling and immersive game experience 
company Maze Theory, supported by £3.12m of 
equity investment.

Launched in 2016 with the aim of creating performance-optimising 
clothing, TESLASUIT has developed a range of products aimed at 
enabling communication between the human body and computer. The 
TESLASUIT, a two-piece full biometric bodysuit of a jacket and trousers, 
has been designed to improve human performance and training for 
complex tasks in settings from industrial to manufacturing to medical.
The company has attended the MassChallenge UK accelerator, a 
programme sponsored by firms such as JPMorgan Chase, Crowdcube, 
and Boston Consulting Group, which facilitates the growth of UK 
startups generating a positive social impact. TESLASUIT has benefitted 
from £8.79m of equity investment across six funding rounds.

y deep-dive: The future of gaming
The gaming industry has displayed 
a distinct ability to mould itself 
to the demands of a generation, 
transforming from a sector defined 
by traditional puzzles and board 
games to one of the UK’s most 
technologically advanced fields. 
Equity investment into this space 
has been strong with high-growth 
companies attracting £1.46b across 
938 fundraising rounds since 2011.
Looking to the future of gaming, 
technological advances suggest 
that gaming will transcend into a full 
or partial virtual reality—providing 
a more immersive experience 
for users and increasing player 
engagement. Companies working in 
the industry have enhanced games 
by stimulating specific sensations or 
tracking eye movements to create an 
individualised adventure.  
When compared with other 
sectors, the gaming industry has 
been praised for its unique ability 
to thrive outside of London—a 
prospect funds are eager to engage 
with as they seek to explore 
regional investment opportunities. 
Businesses such as Build a Rocket 
Boy, based in Edinburgh, and 
Lockwood Publishing, located in 
Nottingham, have attracted large 
valuations—£111m and £92.2m 
respectively—showcasing the 
industry’s potential for high-growth 
outside of the capital.

active high-growth future gaming companies

Improbable develops and designs software 
and technology to underpin virtual gaming 
environments. It provides the necessary 
infrastructure to execute the vision of 
gaming studios.
Launched in 2012 by two computer 
science students from the University 
of Cambridge—Herman Narula and 
Rob Whitehead—the business has 
aimed to create new approach to virtual 
environments.
Improbable has attracted £461m of equity 
funding to advance this aim, attracting 
international investors including the 
Chinese firm NetEase Capital, Japan’s 
Softbank Vision Fund and the Singapore-
based fund Temasek. The company secured 
a valuation of £1.51b during its most recent 
funding round, catapulting Improbable to 
unicorn status. 
Since launching in 2016, Tripledot Studios has amassed a 
wide portfolio of mobile gaming apps including Soduko, 
Blackjack and Solitaire. The company was founded by 
game creators Akin Babayigit, Eyal Chameides, and 
Lior Shiff to reimagine the nature of gaming studios. It 
has secured £63.3m of equity across three fundraising 
rounds. The most recent of these, in April 2021, valued 
the company at £204m, and attracted investors such as 
Access Industries and Lightspeed Venture Partners.
London-based Flexion offers an open and global 
distribution platform for android games, meaning 
developers can distribute games in more channels 
—such as the app stores of Huawei, Amazon, Samsung 
and Xiaomi. Flexion has raised £22.2m across six 
equity rounds since 2014 and also received a €1.90m 
grant in 2016 from Horizon 2020 to broaden the mobile 
applications market and avoid dominance by Google Play.

nDreams develops and publishes games to be used alongside VR 
headsets. Although in operation since the early 2000s, the company 
pivoted to VR in 2013, when they secured early-stage prototypes of 
the Oculus Rift and Playstation headsets, redirecting focus towards 
the immersive space instead.
Priding themselves of combining innovation with excellence, nDreams

funding rounds, securing £11.4m of equity investment from firms 
including Mercia Fund Managers. The most recent of these rounds, in 
October 2020, valued the company at £29.2m.

An emerging subsector is virtual reality 
(VR) with 123 high-growth companies 
currently active in the space. VR refers 
to immersive simulated experiences in 
virtual environments and has applications 
in gaming, entertainment, business and 
education.
VR companies that have raised the most

The Imaginarium Studios. Immersive 
technologies are also being used to 
support learning. EdTech innovators 
include employee knowledge sharing

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is another 
cutting-edge technology revolutionising 
a number of sectors including marketing 
and publishing. WeFarm has developed 
an AI-driven SMS tool to help farmers 
in remote communities to access a 
knowledge network and marketplace.

Sustainability and New Media and Immersive Tech companies
All growing innovative companies, including those in New Media, and 
Immersive Tech need to consider their impact on the climate and the 
importance of sustainability. The video game industry is notoriously 
unfriendly to the environment, consuming staggering amounts of 
energy and hardware being built from plastic and mined materials 
such as gold, copper and zinc. Innovation in gaming could look like 
energy efficient devices, in-game nudges to power off consoles after 
play, and recyclable packaging and reuse of console parts.
In 2019, the UN Environment Programme launched Playing for the 
Planet, an initiative to encourage gaming firms to take these actions 
as well as participate in the environmental agenda through tree 
planting and plastic reduction. Big industry names have joined the 
Playing for the Planet Alliance, including Microsoft, Sony Interactive 
Entertainment, and SEGA.
Sustainability agendas are also being supported by the New 
Media industry in the form of education. Raising awareness for 
environmental concerns can be achieved through gaming, EdTech 
platforms, and perhaps most significantly, social networks. Consumers 
are able to gain more information than ever about the products they 
are purchasing and the materials they are disposing of. Virtual reality, 
augmented reality and Artificial Intelligence may have a role to play in 
transforming education about the planet and research on solutions to 
the climate crisis.
